sentences.text: Martinavis belongs to the group of enantiornithine birds, a diverse lineage of early avians.

The largest known member, M. vincei, measured 51 cm in length and weighed 1.8 kg, while M. saltariensis was slightly smaller at 44.2 cm long and 1.2 kg. A third species, M. whetstonei, was extremely diminutive, reaching no more than half the size of the largest form.
One species grew to a weight of 1.8 kg, making it the heaviest known enantiornithine.
Another species was so small it was at most half the size of the largest relative.
Cyril A. Walker, Eric Buffetaut, and Gareth J. Dyke named the genus in 2007.
The type species, M. cruzyensis, is defined by a complete right humerus discovered in the Grès à Reptiles Formation of France.
Three additional species were described in 2009 from the same location as the type species.
These birds lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils have been found in what is now southern France, North America, and Salta Province, Argentina.
Researchers suggest that some El Brete Martinavis specimens might actually be the same species as other enantiornithines previously described from leg bones.
It is debated whether some Martinavis specimens should be synonymized with Yungavolucris, a foot-propelled swimmer, which would explain the genus's presence in marine environments.
